label: H.R. 2657

latest_action.text: Forwarded by Subcommittee to Full Committee by Voice Vote.
Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini.

summary: H.R. 2657, known as Sammy’s Law, requires large social media platforms to provide real-time programming interfaces that let children under 17 (or their parents or guardians) give third-party safety software providers permission to manage the child's online interactions, content, and account settings. These software providers must register with the Federal Trade Commission, undergo security reviews, and meet strict criteria regarding data usage, privacy, and storage within the United States.

affected_groups.effect: Can permit third-party software providers to manage their accounts, interactions, and settings, and have their data monitored for potential harms.
affected_groups.group: Children under 17 years old with social media accounts

affected_groups.effect: Empowered to delegate management of their child's social media accounts to third-party safety software and receive disclosures if the child faces specific risks.
Required to create and maintain real-time application programming interfaces for safety software and establish secure user data transfer processes.
Must meet strict registration, security review, auditing, data deletion, and domestic storage requirements set by the Federal Trade Commission in order to access platform data.

key_provisions: Large social media platforms (having more than 100 million monthly global active users or generating over $1 billion in gross revenue) must create application programming interfaces to allow third-party safety software access.
Children aged 13 or older, or parents/legal guardians, can delegate permission to a registered third-party software provider to manage account settings, interactions, and content.
Safety software providers must register with the Federal Trade Commission, pass a security review, and store all user data exclusively on hardware inside the United States.

Safety software providers are strictly limited in disclosing user data, except to the parent or guardian if the child experiences or is at risk of specific harms like suicide, eating disorders, sexual abuse, or harassment.

Establishes a single national standard by preventing states and political subdivisions from enacting conflicting laws regarding application programming interfaces for third-party safety software on large social media platforms.
missing_information: Exact civil penalty amounts or fine figures for violations of the Act under FTC enforcement.
The exact effective date of the Act, which depends on when the FTC issues guidance.
summary_detail.plain_summary: H.R. 2657, known as Sammy’s Law, requires large social media platforms to provide real-time programming interfaces that let children under 17 (or their parents or guardians) give third-party safety software providers permission to manage the child's online interactions, content, and account settings. These software providers must register with the Federal Trade Commission, undergo security reviews, and meet strict criteria regarding data usage, privacy, and storage within the United States.
summary_detail.significance: This bill establishes a comprehensive federal framework governing third-party software access to large social media platforms for the protection of minors. It places compliance and enforcement duties on the Federal Trade Commission, sets national uniformity by preempting state-level mandates on the same topic, and limits liability for platforms that comply in good faith.
